Lesson 1 · Understand the problem

Measurement and data preparation

The chain wants fewer empty shelves without paying for unnecessary inventory. Our first job is to establish what the operating reports actually measure.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

The operations director is considering replenishment alerts: a weekly message that asks a store to review low-stock products and bring forward replenishment. Before funding a trial, the director asks how much of the current stockout problem is real. The export has duplicated records, blank counts, and impossible values. The immediate deliverable is a reconciled store-week file with one consistent stockout measure. This file will become the baseline used throughout the course.

Define what the data represent

General theory

A dataset represents a population through defined observations

  • Population: the units and periods the question concerns
  • Observation: what one row represents
  • Variable: a characteristic measured for each observation
  • Frame and sample: the available list and the selected observations

Begin with the question and define its target population. Then choose the observation unit: a person, organization, transaction, or unit-period. The frame is the list from which observations can be collected, and the sample is the subset actually selected. These definitions tell us whose experience a statistic summarizes.

The same entity may appear on several rows when time or events are part of the observation. Repetition of an entity identifier is therefore compatible with a valid dataset; uniqueness must be assessed at the chosen observation level.

A sampling design connects the observed sample to its population

  • Define the population, then check the sampling frame
  • Simple random sampling gives every fixed-size subset the same chance
  • Follow up selected units that do not respond
  • Benchmark sample composition against trustworthy population information

The population is the group about which we want to learn; the frame is the available list from which we select. In a simple random sample without replacement, every subset of the chosen size is equally likely, so every listed unit has the same inclusion probability. Other probability designs can use unequal, known chances. Random selection does not make every realized sample identical to the population.

Trace the sequence: population, frame, selected sample, responding sample. Coverage concerns units missing from the frame; nonresponse concerns selected units whose measurements are not obtained. Compare important characteristics with a registry or another trusted source and investigate the collection process. Repeating collection from the same incomplete frame increases volume while leaving the coverage gap in place.

Measurement quality begins with a common definition

  • Validity: the measure captures the intended concept
  • Reliability: the rule yields consistent measurements
  • Comparability: definitions align across units and periods
  • Coverage: the records represent the intended population

A variable needs an operational definition: what is counted, when it is measured, and which values are allowed. A data dictionary records the units, categories, missing-value codes, and collection process. This agreement turns a business concept into a measure that different analysts can use consistently.

Use six questions to review a proposed measure. Meaning: what does it capture? Validity: does that match the intended concept? Reliability: would repeated measurement be consistent? Comparability: is the same rule used across units and periods? Coverage: who is absent? Selection: are the observed and absent units systematically different? The first four guide measurement; the last two guide the population claim.

Measurement scales determine which arithmetic is meaningful

  • Nominal: categories; count and compare shares
  • Ordinal: ordered categories; compare ranks
  • Interval: meaningful differences; zero is a reference
  • Ratio: meaningful differences and ratios; zero denotes absence

A number can be a label rather than a quantity. Nominal codes support counts, ordinal codes additionally support ordering, and interval scales support meaningful differences. Ratio scales add a meaningful zero. Choose summaries that respect these properties: a mean of identifier codes has no substantive interpretation.

Cross-sections, time series, and panels organize different comparisons

  • Cross-section: different units at one time
  • Time series: one unit across time
  • Panel: the same units across time
  • Choose the structure from the comparison of interest

A cross-section describes differences between units, a time series describes change over time, and a panel supports both perspectives. Aggregating or selecting observations can change the structure. State the resulting observation unit after each transformation so that later analysis uses the correct rows and dependence structure.

Design collection before preparing the file

General theory

A common collection protocol makes measurements comparable

  • Choose a source that records the quantity of interest
  • Align the item, timing, and conditions of comparison
  • Turn broad concepts into questions and scoring rules
  • Train reviewers and specify who is blinded to which information

Sources capture different things. Systems and APIs record transactions, logs, or sensor events; web pages record what is displayed; administrative records reflect an organizational process. Surveys and interviews elicit responses, while experiments assign a change and measure its consequences. Choose the source and collection rule together. To compare online and offline prices, for example, match the same product and pack size at approximately the same time, with consistent treatment of taxes and promotions.

Management quality is a concept that needs an operational measure. Define observable practices, ask consistent questions, and use a scorecard with clear anchors. Train interviewers on the same examples so that a score reflects the practice rather than the interviewer. A possible blinded design has respondents describe routines without seeing scoring thresholds and interviewers score those descriptions without seeing firm performance. These two information restrictions reduce different sources of bias; the study should still explain its purpose and obtain the appropriate participation agreement.

A collection plan assigns purpose, permissions, cost, and ownership

  • Specify the decision, required fields, and collection schedule
  • Confirm permitted use and protect identifiable information
  • Budget collection, follow-up, and quality review
  • Assign an owner and record the source history

Compare collecting new data with reusing an existing source. New collection gives control over definitions and timing but requires staff time, participant effort, and follow-up. An existing source may be faster while requiring work to establish its purpose, coverage, and permitted uses. Make those choices before collecting: identify the needed fields, obtain the applicable permissions or consent, set access and retention rules, and assign responsibility for exceptions.

Attach a short source record: who collected the data; why; when and where; how observations were selected and measured; and what transformations have occurred. Keep variable definitions, units, category codes, valid ranges, and missing-value codes in the codebook. Together, the source record and codebook let a colleague assess both the history of the file and the meaning of its columns.

The four Vs translate data scale into processing requirements

  • Volume: how much data must be stored and processed
  • Velocity: how quickly data arrive and must be used
  • Variety: the different sources, structures, and formats
  • Veracity: the accuracy and credibility of the measurements

Translate each V into a design choice. Volume affects storage and computing capacity. Velocity determines whether processing must happen immediately or can run in batches. Variety determines how tables, text, and nested records are connected. Veracity determines source checks and reconciliation rules. Larger collections are useful when they improve the decision; representativeness still depends on the collection process.

Choose a format to fit that task. CSV and TSV exchange plain tables; Excel supports spreadsheet review; JSON and XML represent nested records; Parquet stores typed columns efficiently for analytical work. Preserve delimiters, encoding, data types, and missing-value conventions when converting formats. The storage format does not define what an observation means.

Organize, combine, and summarize records

General theory

Tidy data and explicit keys make transformations traceable

  • One variable per column and one observation per row
  • A key uniquely identifies an observation
  • Long format stores repeated observations in rows
  • Wide format places repeated measurements in columns

A key can contain more than one variable. Tidy organization separates different observation types into related tables. Long and wide formats can encode the same information, but they make different operations convenient. A reshape should preserve keys, values, and totals; it should not silently aggregate conflicting observations.

An entity identifier should be present and stable as names or operating arrangements change. Prefer an identifier that does not encode changeable information such as a manager or region. A primary key uniquely identifies rows in its own table; a foreign key refers to that key from another table. For example, an organization ID can be unique in a registry and repeated in a transaction table whose own key is a transaction ID.

Resolve names to stable entities before checking duplicate observations

Illustrative identity map: reviewed aliases share a stable ID
Original nameStandard nameEntity ID
North QuayNorth QuayE001
N. QuayNorth QuayE001
North Quay branchNorth QuayE001
North Quay OutletNorth Quay OutletE002

Entity resolution establishes which records refer to the same real-world entity. This illustrative map treats three reviewed aliases as one branch and the outlet as a different branch. Confirm identity with an authoritative registry, address, or other stable attributes; spelling similarity suggests a candidate match rather than establishing identity. Keep the original name alongside the reviewed mapping.

After assigning the entity ID, define the observation key, such as entity plus week, and check duplicate observations. Two aliases can refer to one entity while still describing two valid weeks. Conversely, two records for the same entity-week may repeat the same observation or contain conflicting values. Resolving identity makes that subsequent check meaningful.

Join cardinality determines how many rows a merge can produce

  • One-to-one: unique keys on both sides
  • Many-to-one: repeated left keys, unique right keys
  • Many-to-many: multiple candidate pairs
  • Validate uniqueness, unmatched keys, and row counts

A relational join combines rows using shared keys. The intended relationship determines whether the operation preserves or expands the observation count. Viewed from the opposite side, a many-to-one relationship is one-to-many. Choose left or inner joins according to the population the analysis should retain. When relationships change over time, dates or validity intervals belong in the matching rule.

A pooled rate weights each observation by its exposure

Pooled rate = Σ countᵢ / Σ exposureᵢ = Σ weightᵢ × rateᵢ

A rate divides an event count by the opportunities for that event. Here weightᵢ is exposureᵢ divided by total exposure. Equal exposure makes the simple mean of rates equal to the pooled rate. With unequal exposure, an average unit rate and a pooled opportunity rate summarize different targets.

Grouping changes the observation unit. After aggregation, report the contributing counts and exposure alongside the rate. Eligibility rules, such as a minimum number of reporting periods, define which groups enter the summary.

Make preparation reproducible

General theory

Cleaning is a documented sequence of decisions

  • Preserve and profile the original records
  • Define scope, keys, ranges, and coding rules
  • Resolve missing values, duplicates, and inconsistent relationships
  • Validate the output and retain a repair log

Inspect before changing data. Distinguish a genuine zero from missing information, and an identical duplicate from conflicting records with the same key. Check that headers and subtotals have not entered the observation rows, dates fall within the intended period, and quantities use consistent units. Record which rule was used and what it changed so that another analyst can reproduce the dataset.

Recover, exclude, or impute according to the missing-data problem

  • Recover the recorded value from a trusted source when possible
  • Exclusion changes which observations enter the analysis
  • Imputation supplies an estimate, not an observed value
  • Record the reason, affected observations, and resulting coverage

Begin by investigating why the value is missing. A failed export can sometimes be repaired from an original ledger. If recovery is impossible, excluding incomplete observations makes the calculation describe those retained. If busy units are less likely to report, for example, the retained sample can overrepresent quieter operations. Compare missingness across relevant groups before choosing the analytical sample.

Imputation fills a missing value using a stated rule or model. It can retain rows, but the filled value is inferred and its uncertainty matters in later analysis. Mark imputed values and record the information used. A blank count is not automatically zero, and retaining a denominator while omitting an unresolved numerator changes the rate. In the retail application the ledger permits recovery; this is one solution, not a general assumption that every missing value is recoverable.

Automation is useful when its output can be checked

  • Specify the transformation and expected result
  • Check changed rows, totals, and eligibility
  • Keep executable steps beside the data dictionary
  • Assign responsibility for definitions and exceptions

Code and AI assistance can speed up a clearly specified preparation task. The analyst still needs a checkable contract: the intended input, output, and invariants. Preserve the original data, separate inputs from outputs, and organize the project so that someone else can trace each published number back to its source. Fluent explanations and polished charts do not verify a transformation; check the affected records and let the responsible person approve the business rules.

Begin with the shelf opportunity

Worked application

Worked application: Baseline · weeks 1–8 · all 150 stores. Apply the general method to the shared retail records below.

Each store follows the same 20 products over seven days. That creates 140 scheduled product-days per store-week. One stockout product-day means one of those products was unavailable on that day. It is a count of shelf availability, not a count of customers or units of lost sales.

The key is the pair store_id and week. A store appears in several weeks, and a week contains many stores. Read the rows below as repeated observations on stores. This distinction will matter again when we estimate uncertainty and evaluate an alert policy assigned to whole stores.

Begin with the decision and the evidence

Worked application

The first approval is for the data

  • Decision: should the chain test replenishment alerts?
  • Evidence needed: a comparable measure of shelf availability.
  • Deliverable: a documented baseline that another analyst can reproduce.

The director’s question gives the preparation work a purpose. Each choice—what to collect, whom to include, how to combine records—changes the evidence available for the spending decision. This lesson follows that chain from a source record to a review table.

Different sources answer different operating questions

Choose the source to fit the decision
SourceRetail useCollection choice
Systems and APIsSales, orders, delivery logsWhat event triggers a record?
Web recordsCompetitor prices and availabilityWhich products and times are visible?
Administrative recordsStore registry and staffingHow are openings and changes recorded?
Surveys and interviewsStaff explanations of replenishmentWho answers, and how is the question asked?
ExperimentsTest an alert policyWho receives the offer, and when?

A transaction records an event the system was designed to capture. A survey records an answer to a question. An experiment changes an operating rule and measures what follows. Combine these sources deliberately: agreeing on a source is part of defining the business question, not simply a file-format choice.

Six questions make quality concrete

Agree the measurement protocol
QuestionApply it to shelf availability
MeaningDoes a stockout mean unavailable on the shelf or absent from the warehouse?
ValidityDoes this measure the customer-facing availability we want to improve?
ReliabilityWould two reviewers applying the rule obtain similar counts?
ComparabilityAre products, days, and counting rules consistent across stores?
CoverageWhich stores, products, and trading days are represented?
SelectionAre the stores that fail to report systematically different?

Use these questions to assign work. Operations defines “unavailable”; the data team checks coverage; reviewers reconcile disagreements. A polished chart becomes useful only after the underlying measurement agreement is clear. This is the practical meaning of “garbage in, garbage out.”

Decide which business the file describes

Worked application

More rows cannot repair a missing part of the business

  • Coverage: compare the store list with the operating registry.
  • Nonresponse: compare received and scheduled reports.
  • Benchmark: compare location and delivery-time composition.
  • Random sampling: select from the intended frame with known chances.

Imagine that only stores with reliable scanners send a weekly report. Repeatedly collecting their data adds rows without adding the missing stores. The remedy is to improve collection or define the covered population clearly. For an audit, random selection addresses the selection stage; following up selected stores addresses nonresponse.

Make the table match the question

Worked application

Inspect before filtering

import pandas as pd
raw = pd.read_csv('raw-baseline.csv')
raw.head()
raw.shape
raw.dtypes
raw.isna().sum()

A DataFrame is the table; a Series is one column. head shows example rows, shape reports rows and columns, dtypes shows storage types, and isna counts missing values. Download the CSV from Data & labs for this loading example. The self-contained notebook creates the identical input in its shared setup.

Select columns and rows for explicit reasons

working = raw[['store_id', 'week', 'exposure', 'stockout_days']]
first_weeks = working.loc[working['week'] <= 2]
working.iloc[:3]

A list of names selects columns. loc applies a row rule using labels or a condition; iloc selects by position. Record the before-and-after dimensions when restricting a sample. For categories, value_counts(dropna=False) shows missing labels as well as known groups. Text filters distinguish “Urban” from “urban ” until a documented coding rule reconciles them.

Test the proposed identifier

key = ['store_id', 'week']
missing_keys = raw[key].isna().any(axis=1)
duplicate_keys = raw.duplicated(key, keep=False)
raw.loc[missing_keys | duplicate_keys]

Inspect duplicate-key groups before removing rows. Identical repeated exports can be deduplicated; conflicting counts require a source decision. This export contains known repeated records, and the repair ledger supplies the counts for the flagged observations.

Reconcile the export before calculating a rate

Worked application

The initial export contains 1212 rows. Removing 12 duplicate store-week records leaves 1200. A range check finds 12 records with blank or negative stockout counts. The transaction ledger supplies the corrected counts for those exact keys, preserving all 1200 scheduled store-weeks.

Reconciliation is different from discarding inconvenient rows. An empty count is sent back to its source; a genuine zero remains a valid observation. The repair log records the store, week, and recovered count. A colleague can therefore check how the same store-week moved from the export to the analysis.

Extract from the repair log

Show the same observations in a useful layout

Worked application

Long format keeps the observation in a row

Two stores, two weeks
StoreWeekStockout daysExposure
S001118140
S00129140
S002112140
S00229140

The store-week key is visible in long form. Adding another week means adding rows. This layout is convenient for joining attributes, grouping, plotting time, and fitting the models later in the course.

Wide format makes a small review table

The same four observations in wide form
Storestockout_days_1stockout_days_2exposure_1exposure_2
S001189140140
S002129140140

Wide form places weeks across columns, which can help a manager compare adjacent periods. The information has not changed. Column names now combine a variable with a week, so return to a long structure when the analysis needs one store-week per row.

Set the key, unstack the week, name the columns

small = clean.query("store_id in ['S001','S002'] and week <= 2")
wide = small.set_index(['store_id','week'])[['stockout_days','exposure']]
wide = wide.unstack('week')
wide.columns = [f'{variable}_{week}' for variable, week in wide.columns]

The two column levels after unstack are variable and week. The naming rule makes both visible, for example stockout_days_2. For a one-variable wide table, melt moves week columns back into rows. Validate row keys and totals after either transformation; reshaping should preserve the measured information.

Join tables without changing what a row means

Worked application

Make a many-to-one join prove its claim

stores = world()['stores'][['store_id','lead_days','urban']]
joined = clean.merge(stores, on='store_id', how='left',
    validate='many_to_one', indicator=True)
assert len(joined) == len(clean)
assert joined['_merge'].eq('both').all()

The join retains 1,200 store-weeks. validate checks uniqueness on the store side; indicator reveals unmatched rows. Together with the row-count check, these tests prevent a duplicated store profile from silently multiplying the weekly observations.

A manager can work at several stores or in several periods, so manager_id alone is not a unique staffing-spell key. After the time condition, every included store-week should have exactly one responsible manager. Record gaps or overlapping assignments for review.

An event and an observation need not be the same thing

Illustrative stock-transfer ledger, viewed by store
TransferWeekStoreDirectionSigned units
T0012S002In6
T0012S001Out-6
T0023S003In4
T0023S002Out-4

Two transfers create four valid store-perspective rows: one outgoing and one incoming for each event. The key is transfer_id plus store_id. Removing the second occurrence of a transfer ID would destroy a valid observation. Signed units sum to zero across the chain, providing an additional reconciliation check.

Build a review table at the level of the decision

Worked application

Grouping changes the observation unit

reports = pd.DataFrame(preparation_examples()['reports'])
summary = reports.groupby('store_id').agg(
    weeks=('week','size'), stockouts=('stockout_days','sum'),
    exposure=('exposure','sum'))
summary['rate'] = 100 * summary.stockouts / summary.exposure

This demonstration deliberately takes incomplete submissions from six stores. It leaves the full baseline intact. groupby collects each store’s records; named aggregation counts reporting weeks and adds stockouts and exposure. The output has one row per store, so its key and interpretation have changed.

Show the amount of evidence beside the ranking

Incomplete-submission exercise, sorted from lower to higher stockout rate
StoreWeeks receivedStockoutsExposureRate (%)
S0022212807.50
S00111814012.86
S0058157112014.02
S0038159112014.20
S0048164112014.64
S0068174112015.54

A rate based on one week can move sharply with that week’s events. A review rule requiring at least six weeks makes the reporting requirement explicit. It changes eligibility, so name the resulting shortlist as “stores with at least six reported weeks,” rather than calling it the best stores in the chain.

Apply the eligibility rule before plotting

eligible = summary.loc[summary['weeks'] >= 6]
ranked = eligible.sort_values('rate')
ranked[['weeks','rate']]

For a horizontal bar chart, put the store labels on one axis and the stockout rate on the other, using a shared zero and meaningful units. The chart should describe observed service performance. Delivery conditions, product mix, and the length of observation help explain that performance; later lessons compare those conditions directly.

Keep the denominator attached to the result

Worked application

Across the reconciled file there are 21,407 stockout product-days out of 168,000 scheduled product-days. Dividing the totals gives a baseline rate of 12.74%. A rate puts stores on a common scale; the raw count alone would make a longer reporting period appear worse.

Every store-week has the same 140 opportunities in this case. That makes the mean of store-week rates equal to the rate from pooled counts. If a store later expands its monitored product range, the denominator must travel with the count so that the next report still answers the same question.

The initial business target is a rate at or below 10%. That is a management choice about service, not a statistical estimate. It gives us something useful to compare with the baseline while the financial case for alerts is developed.

Hand over a reproducible piece of evidence

Worked application

Give the project a readable structure

retail-analysis/
  README.txt
  raw/        # original exports and variable dictionary
  clean/      # reconciled tables and repair log
  analysis/   # scripts, figures, and decision memo

Use predictable names such as 2026-11-09_store-week_baseline.csv, stable lower-case field names, and zero-padded sequence numbers when order matters. Separate input paths from output paths. A colleague should be able to find the collection rules and run the pipeline without guessing which file is authoritative.

Diagnose before cleaning

  • Repeated stores, transfers, and joined rows: which are errors?
Discuss, then reveal

Start from the observation definition. Eight store-week rows can be valid; two transfer-perspective rows can be valid. The staffing join needs its period condition and a uniqueness check. Remove only verified repeated records, not every repeated identifier.

A store appears eight times, a transfer appears twice, and a staffing join doubles the row count. Which records should be removed?

Create the first entry in the decision memo

Worked application

Hand over the reconciled file together with its key, rate definition, and repair log. The next analyst should be able to join store attributes to it without multiplying rows. The store table has one row per store; the weekly table has one row per store-week. A many-to-one join is the intended operation.

The director can now ask where the problem is concentrated. A chain-wide percentage establishes scale, but the next spending decision will depend on which stores face the largest operational burden. We carry the repaired rows into Lesson 2 rather than starting with a new dataset.

Update the decision memo

Baseline established: 1,200 store-weeks, a fixed denominator of 140 product-days, and a stockout rate of 12.74%. Use this reconciled file for comparisons; retain the source and repair log with it.

Make the call

A blank stockout count appears in a week with 140 scheduled product-days. What enters the rate calculation?

Compare your reasoning

Recover the count from the ledger before calculating the rate. A blank is unresolved information; the denominator is still 140. The recovered count and the reason for repair stay in the log.

The bigger picture

The transferable method is to turn a question into a measurement contract and a reproducible preparation workflow. It applies to transactions, staffing, customers, and repeated organizational records. Define what a row represents, preserve the denominator, and validate each reshape, join, and aggregation before interpreting a result.

After your decision: open the known answer

The export was created by adding 12 duplicate rows, eight blank counts, and four negative counts to the baseline. Reconciliation recovers the original 1,200 store-weeks exactly.
